name: Smishing

quiz.text: What is smishing?

answers.text: A type of phishing attack that uses SMS or other text messages to deceive victims into revealing sensitive information.
A software program that protects your phone from malware and viruses.
A legitimate security verification method used by banks and corporations.
An encrypted messaging service for secure business communications.

quiz.text: Which of the following are red flags that indicate a text message might be a smishing attempt? (Select all that apply)

answers.text: The message creates a sense of urgency, demanding immediate action to avoid negative consequences.
The message comes from an unknown or unverified sender.
The URL in the message looks similar to but doesn't exactly match the official company domain.
The message is sent during regular business hours and contains proper grammar.
The message asks you to call a phone number that is publicly listed on the company's official website.

quiz.text: If you receive a suspicious text message claiming to be from your company's IT department, what should you do? (Select all that apply)

answers.text: Do not click any links or download any attachments in the message.
Verify the legitimacy by contacting IT through official channels (phone number from company directory, official email).
Report the suspicious message to your IT security department immediately.
Click the link to investigate whether it's legitimate before reporting it.
Reply to the text message asking if it's real.

quiz.text: Which of these are effective measures to protect yourself from smishing attacks? (Select all that apply)

answers.text: Enable Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) on all accounts to add an extra layer of security.
Always manually type official website URLs into your browser instead of clicking links in text messages.
Use strong, unique passwords for each account and update them regularly, especially after suspected breaches.
Click on links in text messages to verify they are legitimate before entering any information.
Share your login credentials with colleagues to speed up workflows during urgent situations.

quiz.text: Why do smishing attackers often use fake login pages that closely mimic legitimate company websites?

answers.text: To test the company's website security and report vulnerabilities.
To create a sense of familiarity and trust, making victims more likely to enter their credentials.
To provide an alternative login method when the official website is down.
To help users remember their passwords by providing a practice login page.

quiz.text: After falling victim to a smishing attack and entering your credentials on a fake website, what immediate steps should you take? (Select all that apply)

answers.text: Wait to see if anything suspicious happens before taking any action.
Immediately change your password using the official company website accessed through a trusted method.
Report the incident to your IT security department with detailed information about the suspicious message and website.
Enable Multi-Factor Authentication if it wasn't already active to add an extra security layer.
Monitor your account for unusual activity such as unauthorized login attempts or data access.

steps.name: Introduction
steps.description: In this training, you'll experience a smishing attack orchestrated by Bob, a cybercriminal aiming to steal your credentials through deceptive tactics.
steps.instructions: Click Next to continue.

steps.name: Receiving the Suspicious Text
steps.note: Smishing attacks use urgent language to create panic. In real life, pause and verify before acting.

message.text: Urgent! Your account has been flagged for unusual activity. Click this link to verify your identity: http://faywickhealth-secure-login.com/verify

highlighterTexts: Examine the message closely. Key red flags include demands for immediate action...
...unknown senders...
...and mismatched URLs.
Reflect on these signs before proceeding.

steps.description: As Alice, your mobile phone suddenly buzzes on your desk, indicating a new text message. Intrigued by the unexpected notification during your busy morning, you pick up the phone to check it.
steps.instructions: Open the mobile phone's messaging app to view the text message.

steps.name: Clicking the Suspicious Link
steps.note: Clicking links in unsolicited texts is risky - they often lead to fake sites designed to steal data. Legitimate companies don't request credentials via text. Always navigate to official sites manually.
steps.description: As Alice, you feel uneasy about the text message but are concerned about the supposed account issue. Pressured by the urgent tone, you decide to open the suspicious link to investigate further.
steps.instructions: Click on the link to continue.

steps.name: Viewing the Fake Login Page
steps.note: Always check the URL carefully – fake sites often use slightly altered domains to fool users.
steps.description:
The link opens a webpage that closely mimics Faywick Health's official login portal, complete with the company's logo, colors, and layout. It prompts you to enter your username and password to "verify" your account.

Bob designed this fake site to trick you into sharing your credentials, exploiting the trust inspired by its professional appearance. The URL, http://faywickhealth-secure-login.com, differs from the official site, but the similarity is deceptive.
steps.instructions: Click Next to continue.

steps.name: Entering Credentials
steps.note: Professional-looking pages can still be fraudulent. Attackers invest heavily in mimicking legitimate sites.
steps.description: As Alice, you're reassured by the familiar look of the webpage and, still worried about the urgent account issue, decide to enter your username and password into the fake login portal to resolve the supposed problem.
steps.instructions: Enter your credentials and submit the login form.

steps.name: Encountering an Error Page
steps.note: Unexpected errors after login attempts are a red flag – in such a case, you should contact IT immediately.
steps.description:
After entering your credentials, the webpage displays an error message: "Unable to verify your account at this time. Our systems are experiencing issues. Please try again later." As Alice, this unexpected error heightens your worry, making you suspect something is wrong with the login process or your account.

Unbeknownst to you, Bob has already captured your credentials and is preparing to misuse them. This error page is a common tactic in smishing attacks to deflect suspicion while the attacker gains access.
steps.instructions: Click Next to continue.

steps.name: Bob Accessing the System
steps.note: Always monitor your accounts for unusual activity. Quick detection can limit damage.
steps.description: Bob now uses the stolen credentials for malicious actions like data exfiltration. This demonstrates the real-world impact of smishing – beyond just login details, it can compromise entire systems.
steps.instructions: Click Next to continue.

steps.name: Receiving the Login Alert Email
steps.note: Legitimate security alerts from IT can help detect breaches. Pay attention to login notifications from your organization.

email.message:
Dear Alice,

We detected an unauthorized login attempt to your Faywick Health account yesterday at 11:45 PM from an unknown IP address. This activity does not match your usual login patterns. Please confirm whether this was you. If not, contact the IT department immediately at it@faywickhealth.com by replying to this email or call (555) 123-4567 to secure your account. Do not share your credentials or click any links until this is resolved.

Best regards,
Faywick Health IT Team
email.subject: Urgent: Suspicious Login Activity Detected

highlighterTexts: The email indicates an unusual login activity and a potential breach, intensifying your concern.
It asks you to contact IT if the login wasn't you.

steps.description: As Alice, you open your email app the next morning and find a login alert email from Faywick Health's IT department.
steps.instructions: Check your mail inbox for the latest updates.

steps.name: Report the Incident
steps.note: Note: Use official channels for reporting - never reply to the suspicious message.

variables.name: report
variables.correctValue:
Dear IT Team,

I received your email about an unauthorized login attempt on my account. I believe this is related to a suspicious text message I received yesterday morning, claiming my account was flagged and directing me to a link (faywickhealth-secure-login.com/verify). I clicked the link, which led to a login page that looked like Faywick Health's portal, and entered my credentials. After submitting, I got an error message saying "Unable to verify your account at this time." I'm concerned my account may have been compromised. Please advise on next steps to secure my account.

Thank you,
Alice

steps.description:
As Alice, alarmed by the login alert email and recalling the suspicious text and error page, you decide to reply to the IT department's email to report the incident.

Reporting is key to mitigation. Describe the incident accurately to help IT respond effectively. Even suspected attacks should be reported.
steps.instructions: Reply to the IT department's email to report the incident.

steps.name: Logging into the Corporate Website
steps.note: Always type URLs manually or use bookmarks - never click links from suspicious messages to access sensitive accounts.
steps.description:
After reporting the incident, you take immediate action to secure your account by logging into the official Faywick Health corporate website to update your password through the secure portal.

To ensure safety, you manually navigate to the official website using your browser, avoiding any links from suspicious messages.
steps.instructions: Use the web browser to open the account settings on the official Faywick Health website and log in using your old credentials.

steps.name: Why Strong Passwords Matter
steps.note: Never reuse passwords across accounts. If one account is compromised, all accounts with the same password become vulnerable.
steps.description:
Before updating her password, Alice takes a moment to understand what makes a password strong and why it matters.

A strong password is the first line of defense against unauthorized access. Weak passwords like "password123" can be cracked in seconds using automated tools.
steps.instructions: Click Next to continue.

steps.name: Creating a Strong Password
steps.note: Use SecureVault to generate and save unique passwords for each account.
steps.description:
A strong password combines uppercase and lowercase letters, numbers, and special characters - with at least 16 characters. Such passwords can take years to crack.

After a suspected breach like the one Alice experienced, updating the password immediately is critical. This ensures the attacker can no longer use the stolen credentials.
steps.instructions: Click Next to continue.

steps.name: Generating a Strong Password
steps.note: Use SecureVault to generate and save unique passwords for each account.
steps.description:
Now it's time to put this knowledge into practice. Alice uses the SecureVault browser extension to create a secure, randomly generated password that meets all the criteria for a strong password.

With the newly generated strong password saved to her vault, she updates her account credentials, ensuring Bob can no longer access her account.
steps.instructions:
Go to your account settings on the Faywick Health website.

Then use the SecureVault extension (the shield icon in the browser toolbar) to generate a strong password. Enable Numbers and Symbols, then click 'Save to Vault' and submit the password change form.

steps.name: Enabling Multi-Factor Authentication
steps.note: MFA makes a stolen password much harder to use on its own - it is one of the most effective account protections available. Phishing-resistant MFA (passkeys or security keys) also stops the real-time phishing kits that can still capture an SMS code.
steps.description:
To add an extra layer of security, Alice decides to enable multi-factor authentication. MFA requires a second form of verification, such as a code sent to her phone, in addition to her password.

This step ensures that future login attempts require additional verification, enhancing account security.
steps.instructions:
Open the multi-factor authentication settings on the Faywick Health website and activate multi-factor authentication.

Then submit Alice's phone number to receive a confirmation code.

steps.name: Receiving the MFA Code
steps.note: Never share MFA codes with anyone - legitimate services will never ask for your verification codes.

message.text: Your MFA setup code is 483920. Enter this code to enable multi-factor authentication. Do not share this code.

steps.description: After providing your phone number, you receive an SMS on your mobile phone containing a MFA verification code from Faywick Health. As Alice, you check the message to retrieve the code, which is needed to complete the MFA setup.
steps.instructions: Open the mobile phone's messaging app to view the MFA code.

steps.name: Applying the MFA Code
steps.note: Always enable MFA when available to protect against credential theft.
steps.description:
With the MFA code in hand, you return to the Faywick Health account settings form and enter the code to confirm MFA setup.

Completing this step ensures that your account now requires a verification code in addition to your password, so a stolen password alone is no longer enough to get in.
steps.instructions: Enter the code in the MFA setup section to confirm activation.

steps.name: Conclusion and Lessons Learned
steps.note: Review your company's policies on phishing and stay vigilant to maintain security.
steps.description:
As Alice, you've completed the training, having experienced a smishing attack orchestrated by Bob. By falling for the urgent text, clicking a fake link, and entering credentials, you allowed Bob to access sensitive company data.

However, through reporting the incident and securing your account with a strong password and MFA, you've learned critical strategies to prevent and mitigate future attacks.
steps.instructions: Click the Next button to complete the training and proceed to the exercise quiz.

description: Text messages skip the sender checks and link scanning that protect email, and a small screen hides a lookalike address. Learn the signs of SMS phishing, verify an alert by opening the official app or website yourself, and report suspicious texts to your security team.

name: Business Email Compromise

quiz.text: What does 'Business Email Compromise' (BEC) refer to?

answers.text: When an employee accidentally sends a confidential email to the wrong person.
A type of phishing attack that specifically targets high-level executives for financial gain.
A sophisticated scam that targets businesses, typically by tricking an employee into transferring money or sensitive data to an unauthorized party.
Compromising an email server to send spam emails to a large number of recipients.

quiz.text: Which of the following are common tactics used in BEC attacks? (Select all that apply)

answers.text: Impersonating a CEO or senior executive requesting an urgent wire transfer to a new vendor.
Compromising an employee's legitimate email account and using it to send fraudulent invoices to customers.
Changing bank account details on a legitimate invoice from a known supplier.
Requesting an employee's personal bank details for a 'bonus payment' via an unofficial email.
Sending a mass email with a link to download free software.

quiz.text: You receive an email from your CEO, which seems urgent, asking you to immediately process a payment to a new supplier for a critical project. What should you do before processing the payment? (Select all that apply)

answers.text: Process the payment immediately, as it's from the CEO and states it's critical.
Reply to the email asking for more details about the supplier and project.
Verify the request using a different communication channel (e.g., a phone call to the CEO's known number, or an in-person conversation) to confirm its legitimacy.
Check the sender's email address for subtle misspellings or unusual domains, and examine the email for grammatical errors or odd phrasing.
Forward the email to the finance department and assume they will handle the verification.

quiz.text: What are potential consequences of falling victim to a BEC attack? (Select all that apply)

answers.text: Significant financial losses for the company due to fraudulent transfers.
Damage to the company's reputation and loss of trust from clients or partners.
Legal and regulatory penalties if sensitive data is compromised.
Increased workload for the IT department as they fix the system.
Improved business relations with new, legitimate suppliers.

quiz.text: Which of these are effective measures an organization can implement to prevent BEC attacks? (Select all that apply)

answers.text: Implementing multi-factor authentication (MFA) for all email accounts.
Establishing and enforcing clear payment verification procedures that require multiple approvals and out-of-band verification for unusual requests.
Regularly conducting security awareness training for all employees, especially those involved in financial transactions.
Deploying email authentication protocols like SPF, DKIM, and DMARC to help detect email spoofing.
Trusting all urgent email requests from senior management without question.

quiz.text: If you receive an email from a vendor requesting a change to their bank account details for future payments, what is the best practice?

answers.text: Update the bank details as requested, assuming the email is legitimate.
Call the vendor on a known, official phone number (not one provided in the email) to verbally verify the change.
Reply to the email asking the sender to confirm the change again.
Forward the email to your personal account for safekeeping.

steps.name: Introduction
steps.description: Last week, Tessaly was acquired by Harwelde Industries, a multinational corporation. The merger has created a whirlwind of activity - new processes, unfamiliar systems, and countless emails from the parent company's various departments.
steps.instructions: Click Next to continue.

steps.name: The Chaos of Transition
steps.note: Mergers and acquisitions create confusion that attackers exploit - new contacts, unfamiliar domains, and rushed processes make verification feel impossible.
steps.description:
Alice's desk is cluttered with merger documents, and her inbox is overflowing with messages from Harwelde employees she's never met before.

The transition has been overwhelming, with new vendor approvals, budget reconciliations, and urgent requests coming in hourly. She barely has time to process everything properly, let alone verify every single communication through official channels.
steps.instructions: Click Next to continue.

steps.name: The Deceptive Newsletter
steps.note: Lookalike domains (harwelde-corp.net vs harweldecorp.net) are a common BEC tactic - always verify the exact domain spelling against known company domains.

email.message: Dear Tessaly Finance Managers, Harwelde Announces Strategic Partnership with Meridian Supply Solutions We're excited to announce a major new partnership with Meridian Supply Solutions, a leading provider of enterprise infrastructure services. This partnership will streamline our supply chain operations across all Harwelde subsidiaries, including your team at Tessaly. The partnership will enable faster project delivery and cost optimization across our technology stack. https://harwelde-corp.net/partnership-with-meridian-supply-solutions Best regards, Harwelde Communications Team
email.subject: [URGENT, FOR FINANCE MANAGERS] - New Partnership Announcement.

highlighterTexts: The email appears legitimate and matches the corporate communications style Alice has been receiving since the merger.
Notice the sender domain: harwelde-corp.net is slightly different from Harwelde's actual domain harweldecorp.net. A subtle difference that's easy to miss.
Alice is usually careful with unfamiliar links in her inbox, but with so much new information to absorb after the merger, she decides to click.

steps.description:
Alice notices a new email in her inbox from 'Harwelde Communications' with the subject line '[URGENT, FOR FINANCE MANAGERS] - New Partnership Announcement.'

She clicks the email since the subject implies it's for her.

The sender's email address appears to be news@harwelde-corp.net , which looks official enough given all the Harwelde domains she's been seeing lately.
steps.instructions: Check your mail inbox for the latest updates.

steps.name: Clicking the Link
steps.description: Alice clicks on the link to read more about the new supplier partnership, thinking it's important to stay informed about parent company developments. The browser opens to what appears to be Harwelde's internal news portal, complete with company branding and recent merger-related articles.
steps.instructions: Click on the link in the email.

steps.name: The Fake Portal
steps.note: Clicking links in phishing emails confirms your email is active and being read - attackers use this to refine their targeting for the main attack.
steps.description:
The article discusses Harwelde's strategic partnership with 'Meridian Supply Solutions' and emphasizes the urgent need to establish payment channels for immediate project implementation. The website looks professional and contains other legitimate-seeming corporate news, making Alice believe this is genuine company information.

What Alice doesn't realize is that this website is fake. By clicking the link, she has unknowingly validated her email address and confirmed she's actively reading communications that appear to be from Harwelde.
steps.instructions: Click Next to continue.

steps.name: The Urgent Financial Request
steps.note: A legitimate email address doesn't mean a legitimate request - compromised accounts are the most dangerous because they bypass domain verification.

email.message:
Alice,

Following today's partnership announcement with Meridian Supply Solutions, we need an urgent $85,000 wire transfer to secure critical infrastructure.
I need you to authorize this wire transfer by end of business today. I'm in board meetings all afternoon discussing the acquisition integration, so I won't be available by phone until tomorrow. Please proceed with the transfer using the details below and send me a confirmation once processed.

I know this is short notice, but the vendor's payment terms are non-negotiable, and any delay will push our implementation into Q1, which would significantly impact our merger success metrics.

Payee: Meridian Supply Solutions LLC, 
Account: 4472-8839-2156-7734, 
Routing: 012345678, 
Bank: First National Commerce Bank, 
Ref: HW-MERIDIAN-Q4-INFRA

Best,
Michael Chen, Finance, Harwelde Industries
email.subject: URGENT: Immediate Payment Authorization Required - Meridian Supply
email.senderName: Michael Chen, Finance Manager - Harwelde Industries

highlighterTexts: The email comes from a legitimate Harwelde address. But a real email address doesn't guarantee the person behind it is who they claim to be.
Bob has been silently monitoring Michael's inbox for weeks, learning about the merger that is happening now. He's ready to strike, using Michael's compromised account.
The email seems legitimate - it references the newsletter she just read, comes from a genuine Harwelde finance email address, and lays out the payment details in a professional format.
Alice decides she should probably verify this request, but she's already running late for a budget meeting, and the email explicitly states it needs to be processed by end of business.
She's torn between following proper verification procedures and meeting what appears to be an urgent corporate deadline from the parent company.

steps.description: Thirty minutes later, Alice receives another email - this time from the legitimate Harwelde email system.
steps.instructions: Check your mail inbox for the latest updates.

steps.name: The Fatal Decision
steps.note: Trust your instincts - if something feels wrong, pause and verify. Urgency and unavailability are classic pressure tactics designed to bypass your judgment.
steps.description:
Against her better judgment, Alice decides to process the transfer. She reasons that the email came from a Harwelde Finance Manager, references the official partnership announcement, and carries an urgent business justification.

With everything happening so quickly since the merger, she assumes this must be part of the new corporate procedures she hasn't been fully briefed on yet.
steps.instructions: Click Next to continue.

steps.name: Accessing Payment System
steps.description: Alice logs into Tessaly's financial portal and initiates a wire transfer for $85,000 to the bank account details provided in Michael Chen's email.
steps.instructions: Open the web browser, go to the company's financial portal, and log in using Alice's credentials.

steps.name: Submitting The Transfer Details
steps.note: Always verify payment requests through a known phone number - never use contact details provided in the request itself.
steps.description: She feels a lingering sense of unease but pushes it aside, telling herself she was following instructions from the parent company's finance leadership.
steps.instructions: Fill out the finance details and submit the form. Then, click Next to continue.

steps.name: The Shocking Phone Call
steps.description: Answer the incoming phone call from CEO James Morrison.
steps.instructions: Listen to the phone conversation and click Next to continue.

steps.name: The Devastating Realization
steps.description: Alice feels the blood drain from her face as James continues.
steps.instructions: Listen to the phone conversation and click Next to continue.

steps.name: Conclusion
steps.note: BEC attacks often involve weeks of reconnaissance - attackers study communication patterns, org charts, and timing to make their requests feel natural.
steps.description:
Alice reflects on the complete attack timeline:

Bob first compromised Michael Chen's Harwelde email account through a phishing attack, then spent weeks silently monitoring internal communications to learn about the merger, corporate procedures, and communication styles.

He used this insider knowledge to send a credible fake newsletter establishing the fictitious Meridian Supply partnership, then leveraged Michael's compromised account to request the fraudulent wire transfer.
steps.instructions: Click Next to continue.

steps.name: Key Takeaways
steps.note: Two-person authorization and out-of-band verification (calling a known number) are your strongest defenses against BEC attacks.
steps.description:
Key prevention measures Alice learned:

- Always verify financial requests through independent voice communication, regardless of the sender's email authenticity.
- Implement multi-person authorization for significant transfers.
- Be aware that legitimate email accounts can be compromised and used for fraud.
- Establish clear verification procedures that can't be bypassed by claims of urgency or unavailability.

This sophisticated Business Email Compromise attack nearly cost the company $85,000 and demonstrated how account takeover attacks represent one of the most dangerous forms of email fraud.
steps.instructions: Click Next to continue.

description: Business email compromise uses a trusted name and a sense of urgency to get money moved, with no malicious link or attachment for a filter to catch. Learn to inspect the real sender address, verify payment requests on a separate channel, and rely on controls such as two-person authorization for transfers.

name: Double Barrel Phishing

quiz.text: What does 'Double Barrel Phishing' refer to in the context of cybersecurity?

answers.text: An attack that uses two different email accounts to send a single phishing message.
A sophisticated phishing attack that uses two distinct stages or vectors, often building trust or gathering information in the first stage before delivering the main malicious payload in the second.
A phishing email that contains two different links to the same fake login page.
An attack that targets two different departments within an organization simultaneously.

quiz.text: Which of the following scenarios best describes a 'Double Barrel Phishing' attack? (Select all that apply)

answers.text: An attacker sends a seemingly harmless email (e.g., a survey or an internal policy update) to gauge recipient engagement and verify active email addresses, followed by a more malicious email with malware or a credential harvesting link.

An attacker first compromises a less critical account (like a personal social media profile) of an employee to gather information, then uses that information to craft a highly convincing phishing email for their corporate account.
An attacker sends two identical phishing emails from the same sender address to the same recipient, hoping one gets through spam filters.
A hacker gaining access to your personal email and then your work email through the same phishing link.
An attacker uses a generic phishing email to collect credentials, and then uses those credentials to log in to the victim's account directly.

quiz.text: Why are Double Barrel Phishing attacks often more successful than standard phishing attempts?

answers.text: They target a much wider audience, increasing the chances of a successful click.
They create a false sense of security or legitimacy in the initial stage, making the victim less suspicious of the follow-up attack.
They rely solely on advanced technical exploits that bypass all security software.
They use sophisticated encryption that prevents detection by email filters.

quiz.text: You receive an email from an external vendor asking for feedback on a recent service, with a link to a survey. A week later, you receive another email from the same 'vendor' referencing your participation in the survey and offering a 'thank you' discount, asking you to click a new link to claim it. What might this indicate?

answers.text: A legitimate follow-up from a grateful vendor.
A standard marketing campaign.
A potential Double Barrel Phishing attempt, where the first email was to establish trust or verify your email, and the second is the malicious payload.
The vendor is simply trying to confirm your identity.

quiz.text: Which of these measures are particularly important for defending against Double Barrel Phishing attacks? (Select all that apply)

answers.text: Maintaining a high level of skepticism for all unsolicited communications, even those that seem less threatening initially.

Verifying the legitimacy of the sender and any links through independent means (e.g., calling the organization directly, using official websites) rather than relying on information in the email itself.
Enabling Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) on all critical accounts to provide an extra layer of security even if credentials are stolen.
Disabling your email's spam filter so you don't miss any important communications.
Ignoring all emails that come from external senders.

quiz.text: What distinguishes Double Barrel Phishing from a typical, single-stage phishing attack?

answers.text: It always involves a phone call in addition to an email.
It uses a two-step approach, often with a less suspicious initial interaction followed by a more direct malicious one, to bypass defenses and build rapport.
It targets only high-level executives.
It relies on sending the exact same malicious link twice in a row.

steps.name: Introduction
steps.note: Attackers often research targets on LinkedIn and social media to craft personalized attacks. Be mindful of what professional information you share publicly.
steps.description: Quillmarsh Consulting specializes in connecting talented professionals with clients. You manage a comprehensive database containing sensitive candidate information including resumes, contact details, salary expectations, and personal data.
steps.instructions: Click Next to continue.

steps.name: The Unexpected Call
steps.description: Alice is reviewing applications at her desk when her phone rings. The caller sounds professional and articulate, introducing himself as 'David Miller', a senior software engineer interested in opportunities at Quillmarsh Consulting.
steps.instructions: Listen to the phone conversation and click Next to continue.

steps.name: The Attack Begins
steps.description: During the phone call, Bob (as David) presents himself as an articulate and knowledgeable professional. The conversation flows naturally as they discuss his background, the role requirements, and company culture. About halfway through the call, Bob steers the conversation in a seemingly innocent direction.
steps.instructions: Click Next to continue.

steps.name: Gathering Intelligence
steps.note: Attackers use casual conversation to extract valuable information. Questions about tools, software, or internal processes may seem harmless but help attackers craft convincing follow-up attacks.
steps.description: Alice is being asked what seems like an innocent question.
steps.instructions: Listen to the phone conversation and click Next to continue.

steps.name: The Email Exchange
steps.description:
After the positive phone conversation, Alice sends Bob, disguised as 'David', detailed information about several open positions that match his background. 

Alice wants to enter David's details into the TalentHub Pro database because he seems like a very suitable candidate and she can get a hiring bonus. So she eagerly awaits his response email with his resume.
steps.instructions: Click Next to continue.

steps.name: The Preparation
steps.note: Double-barrel attacks use an initial contact to gather intelligence (like which tools you use), then weaponize that information in the second attack.
steps.description: Meanwhile, Bob prepares a fake TalentHub Pro login page. He has already created urgency for Alice to use TalentHub Pro and is now ready to exploit it.
steps.instructions: Click Next to continue.

steps.name: The Phishing Email Arrives
steps.note: Attackers create lookalike domains (quillmarsh-consulting-secure.com vs quillmarsh.com) that appear legitimate at a glance. Always verify the exact domain in unexpected IT requests.

email.message: Dear Alice, Please complete your account migration immediately using the secure link below. This migration is necessary to protect against the recently discovered security vulnerability. Failure to complete this process by 5:00 PM today will result in temporary account suspension until the migration can be completed manually by our IT team. http://talenthub-pro-migration.quillmarsh-consulting-secure.com/login Best regards, IT Support
email.subject: URGENT: TalentHub Pro Security Migration Required

highlighterTexts: Alice is shocked. She can't afford being suspended because she needs to process the data of the ideal candidate any minute now.
Email sender's domain quillmarsh-consulting-secure.com is different from the official portal workspace.quillmarsh.com, but Alice is in a hurry.
Without hesitation, Alice clicks the link. This is exactly what Bob is counting on.

steps.description: Alice receives an email that appears to be from the company's IT department. The sender address shows it-support@quillmarsh-consulting-secure.com and includes the familiar company logo and professional formatting that Alice recognizes from legitimate IT communications.
steps.instructions: Open your email inbox and read the new message from IT Support, then click Next.

steps.name: Reading the Email
steps.description:
Alice clicks on the migration link, which opens what appears to be the TalentHub Pro login page. The website looks identical to the system she uses daily: same colors, logo, layout, and familiar interface elements.

The URL displays 'http://talenthub-pro-migration.quillmarsh-consulting-secure.com/login', but Alice is too rushed to notice the missing HTTPS encryption.
steps.instructions: Click on the link in the email.

name: Callback Phishing

quiz.text: What is callback phishing (TOAD)?

answers.text: A phishing attack where the victim receives a call from the attacker.
A phishing attack where the victim is tricked into calling the attacker's phone number.
A type of email phishing that requests a callback.
An automated robocall that steals information.

quiz.text: Why is callback phishing particularly effective? (Select all that apply)

answers.text: Victims feel safer because they initiated the call themselves.
Human interaction over the phone builds trust more effectively than emails.
Urgency about fraud or security issues bypasses critical thinking.
Phone calls cannot be traced by law enforcement.

Call the official number on the back of your card or from your bank's official website.

Reply to the email to ask for more details.

The last four digits of your card (for verification).
Your name as it appears on the card.

Call your real bank to report the compromise and request new cards.
Change passwords for any accounts whose credentials were compromised.
Wait 24-48 hours to see if any unauthorized charges appear.
Call the scammer's number back to demand they delete your information.

Notice the urgency tactics: "URGENT" subject line, threat of account suspension, and a 24-hour deadline to pressure immediate action.
The email provides a phone number to call rather than a link to click. This is the hallmark of callback phishing (TOAD) - making the victim initiate contact.

steps.instructions: Enter your corporate card details as directed by the support agent.

steps.name: The Final Piece

steps.name: Something Feels Wrong
steps.description:
Alice stares at her phone. The call ended so suddenly. And now that she thinks about it - shouldn't they have been able to see her account information already? Why did they need her to enter everything manually on a website?

She decides to call the number on the back of her actual corporate card.
steps.instructions: Open your phone contacts and call the real Corporate Card Services.

steps.name: Understanding the Attack
steps.description:
The real Corporate Card Services representative confirmed Alice's worst fears: there was no fraudulent charge on her account. The email, the phone number, and "Michael" were all part of an elaborate callback phishing scheme. Callback phishing - also known as TOAD (Telephone-Oriented Attack Delivery) - is particularly effective because:
  • You initiate contact - Calling a number feels safer than clicking a link
  • Human interaction builds trust - A helpful voice is more convincing than an email
  • Urgency bypasses caution - Fear of fraud overrides critical thinking
  • Information is gathered incrementally - Each small request seems reasonable

name: Phishing Awareness

quiz.text: What is 'phishing' in the context of cybersecurity?

answers.text: A type of malware that encrypts files and demands a ransom.
The act of attempting to trick individuals, usually via email, into revealing sensitive information or clicking malicious links.
Unauthorized access to a computer system or network.
A method of spreading fake news on social media.

quiz.text: Which of the following are common indicators that an email might be a phishing attempt? (Select all that apply)

answers.text: Urgent or threatening language demanding immediate action.
Generic greetings like 'Dear Customer' instead of your name.
Requests for sensitive personal information (passwords, credit card numbers) directly in the email or via a linked form.
A display name that does not match the sender's actual email address.
A sender email address that perfectly matches the legitimate organization's domain.
Links that, upon hovering, show a different URL than what is displayed.

quiz.text: You receive an email from a well-known online retailer claiming there's a problem with your recent order and asking you to click a link to update your payment information. What should you do?

Reply to the email asking for more details about the problem.
Do not click the link. Instead, go directly to the retailer's official website (by typing the URL or using a bookmark) and log in to check your order status.
Forward the email to the retailer's customer service to ask if it's legitimate.

quiz.text: What potential consequences can arise from falling victim to a phishing attack? (Select all that apply)

answers.text: Compromise of your email or other online accounts.
Financial loss through fraudulent transactions.
Installation of malware (e.g., viruses, spyware) on your device.
Identity theft.
Your computer performing faster due to a 'security update'.

quiz.text: Which of the following are effective ways to protect yourself from phishing attacks? (Select all that apply)

answers.text: Be skeptical of unsolicited emails and messages, especially those with urgent requests or suspicious links.
Always verify the sender's email address and hover over links to check their true destination before clicking.
Use strong, unique passwords for different accounts and enable Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) whenever possible.
Report suspicious messages to your IT or security team instead of just deleting them.
Disable your email's spam filter to ensure you receive all messages.

quiz.text: If you accidentally click on a suspicious link in a phishing email, what is the best immediate action?

answers.text: Enter your login credentials if prompted, as you're already there.
Close the browser tab/window immediately, scan your device for malware, and change any potentially compromised passwords.
Forward the email to your entire contact list to warn them.
Nothing, as long as you didn't download anything, you're safe.

steps.name: How SEO Poisoning Works

highlighterTexts: Attackers purchase search engine ads to place malicious sites above legitimate results. The small "Sponsored" label is easy to overlook.
These ads often mimic the real vendor's branding and use keywords like "official download" or "free trial" to appear trustworthy.
Beyond paid ads, attackers use keyword stuffing, link farms, and stolen content to artificially boost malicious pages in organic rankings.
Some attackers even compromise legitimate high-ranking websites and inject hidden redirects to their malicious download pages.

steps.name: Protecting Yourself

highlighterTexts: Always use your company's software request process to install new tools. IT can verify the source and handle installation safely.
If you need to search, navigate directly to the vendor's known official website by typing the URL manually or using a saved bookmark.
Before clicking any search result, check the domain shown below the title. The official vendor domain should match what you expect.
Be especially cautious of "Sponsored" results. Scroll past ads to find organic results ranked by the search engine's algorithm.

steps.name: Key Takeaways
steps.description:
Alice has completed the SEO Poisoning Awareness training. Here are the key lessons from this experience: Before you download:
  • Use your company's approved software request process - never download tools based on casual advice or search results alone
  • Verify the domain in search results before clicking - look for the official vendor URL, not lookalike domains
  • Be skeptical of "Sponsored" results - anyone can buy ad placement, including attackers
Red flags to watch for:
  • Download pages using HTTP instead of HTTPS
  • Recently registered domains or domains that don't match the official vendor
  • Urgency tactics, inflated download counters, and generic testimonials
If something goes wrong:
  • Never dismiss antivirus warnings - report them to IT Security immediately
  • File an incident report as quickly as possible to limit the damage
  • Speed matters - the security team's fast isolation of the workstation stopped lateral movement across the network
